ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: On the left side of the figure is Bus A, with circuit breakers 1 and 2 nearby; the vertical bus in the middle is Bus B, with circuit breakers 3, 4, and 5 along the line, among which circuit breaker 4 is labeled as stuck breaker; on the right side is Bus C, with circuit breakers 6 and 7 nearby. The fault point F is marked near the middle of the transmission line between Bus B and Bus C. Reasoning: The faulty element is the transmission line between Bus B—Bus C. The primary protection for this line fault should first remove the related circuit breakers at both ends of the faulty line; but the problem states that circuit breaker 4 fails to operate, so 4 cannot be taken as an actual operating circuit breaker. According to the given coordination idea, the next coordinated backup on the Bus B side is circuit breaker 5, so 5 operates first. Then on the Bus C side, according to the coordination sequence, 6 and 7 operate to remove the remote-end power supply of the faulty line. After that, the higher-level backup on the Bus B side is 3, and further toward the remote Bus A side the backups are 1 and 2 in sequence. Therefore one effective operating sequence is 5, 6, 7, 3, 1, 2.

method.method_draft: First identify the faulted element in the image as the Bus B-Bus C transmission line at F. The primary clearing devices would be the breakers at the ends of the faulted section, including breaker 4 on the Bus B side, but the text says 4 is stuck, so omit it and use the next coordinated Bus B-side backup, breaker 5, as the earliest actual operation. Then trip the Bus C-side devices in their coordinated order, 6 then 7, to isolate the remote side of the faulted line. After those, use the next upstream backup on Bus B, breaker 3, and finally the still more remote Bus A backups, 1 then 2. This yields the valid operating sequence 5, 6, 7, 3, 1, 2.
